extracted.intended_audience: students, travelers, and readers interested in architecture, art history, and ecclesiastical/Byzantine art
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and design principles from Ruskin's discussion of St. Mark's and Byzantine palaces — including iconographic program, didactic function, material/ornament justification, and subtle proportional rules of composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance in religious art (avoid extremes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective religious art... has always lain... between the two extremes--of barbarous idol-fashioning on one side, and magnificent craftsmanship on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious art should avoid the crude literalism of 'idol-fashioning' and the merely ostentatious display of technical perfection that withdraws attention from spiritual meaning. Ruskin situates productive religious art between simple/traditional representation and high craftsmanship capable of conveying doctrine and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of inlaying and mosaic (12th–13th centuries)
rubrics_metrics.description: But of all these branches the most important are the inlaying and mosaic of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, represented in a central manner by these mosaics of St. Mark's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mosaics should cover walls and roofs so they are unavoidable in worship; their size makes them majestic, their distance makes them mysterious, and their color attractive. They should not degenerate into mere page-ornamentation or be overworked with evidences of scientific skill that distract from subject-matter. Examples invoked: Baptisteries of Parma and Florence; domes of Venice and Pisa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as didactic 'stone manuscript' — inscriptions must be readable
rubrics_metrics.description: Our eyes are now familiar and wearied with writing... the old architect was sure of readers... We must take some pains, therefore, when we enter St. Mark's, to read all that is inscribed...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural inscriptions and pictorial programmes are intended to be read and deciphered by the public; lettering should be large and clear and inscriptions abundant. The building functions as a 'book' for teaching doctrine and preparing the faithful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programmatic narrative sequencing for catechumens
rubrics_metrics.description: A large atrium or portico is attached... a space which was especially reserved for unbaptized persons and new converts... to contemplate the great facts of the Old Testament history... closing with the Fall of the Manna... to mark to the catechumen the insufficiency of the Mosaic covenant for salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spatial program must be pedagogically ordered: sequence scenes so they instruct viewers (especially newcomers) toward a theological conclusion. Placement (e.g., atrium for pre-baptismal instruction, main entrance/back-reading after baptism) is integral to meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconographic placement to support worshipper experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The mosaic of the first dome... represents the effusion of the Holy Spirit... From the central symbol... twelve streams of fire descend upon the heads of the twelve apostles... groups of two figures for each separate people... angels each bearing a tablet with 'Holy' and 'Lord' and the hymn continued around the border of the dome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iconography should be organized by dome/area to express distinct theological themes (e.g., sanctification, ascension, witness of the Old Testament). Text and image should be integrated (inscriptions, hymns, captions) so viewing/worship becomes participation in doctrine; symbolism (dove, tongues of fire, angels' tablets) must be legible and theologically coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on core Christian facts through imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The worshipper should be led to contemplate... that Christ died, that He rose again, and that He ascended into heaven... The second cupola... is entirely occupied by the subject of the Ascension... the centre of the church... fixes the mind of the worshipper on the main groundwork and hope of Christianity,--'Christ is risen,' and 'Christ shall come.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic imagery must prioritize and repeatedly assert the central salvific events (crucifixion, resurrection, ascension). The scale and placement of imagery (central cupola, principal vaults) transmit theological hierarchy so that even brief visitors receive key messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration must serve theological message, not secular vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Not in the wantonness of wealth, not in vain ministry to the desire of the eyes or the pride of life, were those marbles hewn into transparent strength... There is a message written in the dyes of them, that once was written in blood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of expensive materials and lavish ornamentation is justified only when it testifies to divine truth and aids worship; ornamentation as civic or private vanity undermines moral and religious purpose. Ruskin warns that sin committed 'in the face of the House of God' is greater because the building's message heightens culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle harmony of proportion as a hallmark of Byzantine workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: These singular and minute harmonies of proportion indicate... that the buildings in which they are found are of one school... the subtlety of the feeling for proportion in the Greek architects... differences of a few inches were intentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess quality and authorship by careful measurement of proportional relationships (arc widths, gradations from center to flanks, repetition/echo of shafts). Small variations (inches) are deliberate refinements that create visual cadence; precision and subtle gradation are evidence of high artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous arcades and tiered arch composition
rubrics_metrics.description: They all agree in being round-arched and incrusted with marble... these six agree farther in having continuous arcades along their entire fronts... having their arcades divided... into a centre and wings; tall and few arches in their lower stories, and shorter and more numerous arches above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristic formal rules include continuous arcades, central-dominant composition (centre + wings), and a vertical organization of arches (fewer/taller at bottom, more/shorter above). These features serve as diagnostic criteria for identifying Byzantine palaces and for composing in the style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of apparently non-functional elements to consummate proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Byzantine builder could not be satisfied with so simple a group, and he introduced, therefore, two minor arches at the extremities... by adding two small porticos which are of no use whatever except to consummate the proportions of the façade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal completeness sometimes requires adding purely compositional elements. Evaluate façades not only by functional necessity but by their role in completing proportion and visual rhythm; non-functional additions can be essential to harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity indicated by preserved subtle proportional coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: No modern builder has any idea of connecting his arches in this manner, and restorations in Venice are carried on with too violent hands to admit of the supposition that such refinements would be even noticed in the progress of demolition, much less imitated in heedless reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether work is original Byzantine or a later restoration, look for fine proportional coincidences and minute harmonies. Their presence argues for original workmanship; restorations often disrupt these subtleties. Comparative measurement across buildings strengthens attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of pictorial tradition as evidence of intentional iconography
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not mean that modern Christians believe less in the facts than ancient Christians, but they do not believe in the representation of the facts as true... in the Greek Church all painting is, to this day, strictly a branch of tradition... 'Le costume des personnages est partout et en tout temps le même... jusque pour le nombre et l'épaisseur des plis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess images for adherence to established iconographic conventions (costume, color, drawing, number and thickness of folds). Consistency across sites and time indicates a deliberate traditional program rather than individual painterly invention; such continuity is a virtue in Byzantine ecclesiastical painting.
